verdict.headline: Good water evidence — approvals decide this tract
verdict.detail: All 4 nearby records report yields of 0.5–425 gallons per minute (depths 423–663 ft where recorded). That is encouraging per-well evidence — but this is a 25.75-acre tract, not a single homesite. Whether water works here gets answered lot by lot, and only after the question that actually gates this parcel: what can legally be built, how many lots, and whether each lot can carry its own well and septic. Treat the aquifer as one box checked; subdivision approval, layout, and per-lot septic feasibility decide the deal. The record only covers wells filed online since 2021, so treat it as evidence, not a guarantee. The neighbors' wells also stand deep (typical standing reserve about 700 gal in the bore), so the reserve behind those yields is real, not just a strong test day.

well_strength.note: 4 neighbor tests on file record resting levels of 10–60 ft and levels during the test of 423–663 ft; methods: bailing, compressed air; test durations: 4–5 hours. Borehole storage: wells here also stand deep — the typical neighbor well holds about 700 gallons of water standing in the bore itself (about 476.5 ft of water column), a reserve that can carry a house through showers and laundry while the well refills. Each filing records a single endpoint level, so sustained yield is unestablished from these records.

nearby_wells.planning_note: Plan against the geology, not the average: budget for the deep end of the local depth range and price the dry/low-yield downside (+$10k-$25k contingency) before committing.

cost_band_usd.dry_hole_note: You pay for the attempt: drillers bill per foot whether or not the hole produces, so a failed hole at the depths common around here can run about $9,000 to $18,000 at the plan-on rate, before you decide whether to deepen it, hydrofracture it, or drill again somewhere else. Carry a $10,000 to $25,000 contingency for that — our planning allowance, built from the rates above, not a published figure.

flags.title: Water quality — the state panel covers it
flags.summary: Connecticut requires arsenic and uranium testing on every new well — the two contaminants that actually show up in CT bedrock — so the lab runs the state panel as routine. Radon is optional; ask the lab whether to add it, and get the panel price when you book.
flags.detail: Water Quality Portal: 861 uninterpreted regional arsenic sample rows within 25 miles — not a parcel finding. CT DPH/USGS private-well study: 3.9% of sampled CT wells exceeded the arsenic MCL. Water Quality Portal: 2527 uninterpreted regional uranium sample rows within 25 miles — not a parcel finding. CT DPH/USGS private-well study: 4.7% exceeded the uranium MCL. No queryable public result dataset for radon in water found.

water_quality.source: Water Quality Portal (EPA/USGS) Result search, CSV
water_quality.note: Counts are regional sample rows, not parcel predictions. Connecticut requires arsenic and uranium testing for newly constructed private and semipublic wells (CT DPH, effective Oct 1, 2022) — confirm the exact panel with a certified lab.
water_quality.final_word: Risk flags are not a prediction. Laboratory testing of the finished well is the final word.

setbacks.rule: Well to septic system and its leaching field (where septic water drains into the soil), buried oil tank, or other pollution source
setbacks.condition: Well with a required withdrawal rate under 10 gpm — the band a single-family home sits in.
setbacks.scales_with: Bands follow the well's required withdrawal rate (what it serves), not its tested yield: 150 ft if the supply must deliver 10-50 gpm (e.g. one well serving several homes), 200 ft above 50 gpm. A single home sits in the under-10 band.

setbacks.condition: Tight-joint sewer only; well with a required withdrawal rate under 10 gpm.
setbacks.scales_with: Bands follow the well's required withdrawal rate (what it serves), not its tested yield: 150 ft if the supply must deliver 10-50 gpm (e.g. one well serving several homes), 200 ft above 50 gpm. A single home sits in the under-10 band.

setbacks.rule: Well to the leaching system (where septic water drains into the soil) IF the soil is fast AND the ledge is shallow — the distance doubles
setbacks.condition: Applies when BOTH hold: soil percolation rate faster than 1.0 minute per inch, AND the bottom of the leaching system is less than 8 ft above ledge rock. For a single-family home the 75 ft distance becomes 150 ft. Only soil tests on the lot can settle whether this applies — it cannot be screened from public data.
setbacks.source: CT DPH Technical Standards for Subsurface Sewage Disposal Systems, Table 1 Item A (applied to wells via Reg. 19-13-B102d)

setbacks.rule: Well to property boundary — district guidance: keep 25 ft 'if possible' (guidance, not a state setback)
setbacks.condition: NCDHD's subdivision plan-review requirements say no well should be located closer than 25 ft to a property boundary 'if possible'. It is published guidance in a plan-review document — present it as guidance the district will look for, never as a state setback, and note no B51d well-to-property-line distance exists.
setbacks.source: NCDHD Subdivision Plan Review Requirements, item 5 (Rev. 06/30/26)

permit_authority: the North Central District Health Department (NCDHD)

permit_roadmap.step: Before you commit: get driller quotes
permit_roadmap.detail: Get 2–3 quotes from Connecticut-licensed well drillers. Ask each one: what depth would you permit for this lot, and what exactly do I pay if the hole comes up dry?
Well drillers must hold a Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection license. Check it before you sign anything — an unlicensed driller can't pull your permit.

permit_roadmap.who: Your driller files it; you pay the fee
permit_roadmap.detail: Your driller signs the state permit application as applicant and files it with the North Central District Health Department (NCDHD). The fee is set by the district, not the state: it is $200 in the North Central District and $150 in Bloomfield's district, to give the local range. Confirm the current fee with the district before the driller files. Nothing gets drilled before this is approved.

permit_roadmap.step: Pass the site and setback review
permit_roadmap.detail: The district confirms the proposed well spot meets CT setbacks (Public Health Code §19-13-B51d): 75 ft from septic and other pollution sources for a typical home well — the band follows the home’s required withdrawal rate (its water demand), not the well’s tested yield; the 150 ft band is for larger or shared supplies that must deliver 10–50 gpm, and 200 ft above 50 gpm. Plus 25 ft from surface water and drains (50 ft in the higher bands). One rule can change this number: if the soil drains very fast (perc faster than 1 minute per inch) and ledge rock is shallow (leaching bottom less than 8 ft above it), the state doubles the well-to-septic distance — 150 ft for a typical home. That is only known after a perc test, which happens at permit time. This is the step that kills bad lot layouts — better to learn it now than after you own the lot.
You pay for the attempt whether the hole comes up wet or dry — that's why the cost band in this snapshot carries the dry-hole contingency. Get the driller's dry-hole policy in writing.

Every new CT well must be lab-tested on the state-required baseline panel — 15 tests, including arsenic and uranium (CGS 19a-37(c)(2), since October 1, 2022). If the well serves an existing structure, a first-draw lead sample from the plumbing is also required. Ask the lab whether radon testing makes sense for your lot too — the water section above flags what your area's geology suggests.

permit_roadmap.step: Get the health authority's compliance determination
permit_roadmap.detail: The lab results go to your local health authority, which determines whether they comply with the state maximum contaminant levels. The well may not be used for domestic purposes until the health authority makes that determination (CGS 19a-37(c)(2)).
Get a copy of the well completion report your driller files with the state, and keep it with the deed. Future buyers — and future you — will want it.
